lessons.title: TLS 1.3 hybrid post-quantum key exchange through proxy-mode SSL deep inspection
lessons.body_html:
Purpose and inspection boundary

Post-quantum cryptography is not just a VPN concern. A TLS 1.3 client can now offer a hybrid key exchange that combines a conventional elliptic-curve component with a post-quantum ML-KEM component. FortiOS 8.0 adds support for these hybrid exchanges inside proxy-mode SSL deep inspection, so a security gateway does not have to choose between decrypting traffic for inspection and reaching a server that requires a hybrid PQC handshake.

In proxy inspection, FortiGate terminates the client TLS connection and originates a separate server-side TLS connection. That split matters: there are two ClientHello/ServerHello negotiations, two certificate-validation decisions, and two cryptographic contexts. A successful client-facing handshake alone does not prove the upstream server-facing leg negotiated the expected group. Inspect both sides when validating a migration.

Supported exchanges and protocol scope

The documented hybrid groups are X25519MLKEM768 (0x11EC), SecP256r1MLKEM768 (0x11EB), and SecP384r1MLKEM1024 (0x11ED). FortiOS also supports pure ML-KEM groups. The guide documents hybrid plus ML-KEM support for HTTPS, DNS over TLS, POP3, IMAPS, and SMTPS during deep inspection. Hybrid plus ML-KEM and pure ML-KEM are also supported when these protocols run through virtual-server or explicit-proxy modes.

Do not infer that every FortiGate TLS consumer inherits the same support. The guide explicitly calls out SIP over TLS and the URL-filter TLS connection to FortiGuard as not yet supporting hybrid plus ML-KEM. A generic TLS success test can therefore hide a protocol-specific gap.

Configuration pattern

Start from a cloned deep-inspection profile rather than changing a production profile in place. Add any nonstandard test ports to the HTTPS protocol-port mapping, add those ports to the firewall service, then attach the cloned profile to a policy using proxy inspection.

config firewall policy
    edit 1
        set srcintf "port2"
        set dstintf "port1"
        set action accept
        set srcaddr "all"
        set dstaddr "all"
        set schedule "always"
        set service "ALL"
        set utm-status enable
        set inspection-mode proxy
        set ssl-ssh-profile "PQC-deep-inspection"
        set logtraffic all
        set nat enable
    next
end

For a controlled lab, the Fortinet example adds TCP ports 6000-6005 to the HTTPS profile mapping and service, then tests a PQC-enabled web endpoint and DNS over TLS. In production, keep the service object narrow and make sure clients trust the inspection CA; otherwise a certificate warning can be mistaken for a PQC negotiation failure.

Evidence and interpretation

  • A packet capture showing X25519MLKEM768 in ClientHello proves that the client offered that hybrid group; it does not by itself prove the upstream leg negotiated it.
  • Capture the FortiGate-to-server leg separately, or inspect the server-side TLS handshake, to verify the negotiated group at the origin.
  • Successful application traffic through the proxy proves the configured inspection path worked for that protocol and port, not that unsupported TLS consumers are covered.
  • Compare a no-inspection baseline with the proxy-inspected path to isolate server compatibility from certificate trust and policy matching.

Failure isolation and operational caveats

If a browser succeeds without inspection but fails with the proxy profile, verify the policy actually selects proxy mode, the destination port is included in the profile mapping, and the FortiGate has a trusted inspection certificate. Then check whether the origin offers a supported hybrid group. If only one protocol fails, compare the documented support matrix before weakening inspection globally. Keep a rollback profile and test HTTPS, DoT, mail protocols, virtual-server traffic, and explicit-proxy traffic independently during an upgrade. The operational objective is not merely “TLS works”; it is to prove the correct cryptographic exchange on each inspected leg while preserving the inspection controls.

lessons.title: Device blueprints with certificate templates for offline model devices and HA clusters
lessons.body_html:
Purpose and object model

A FortiManager Device Blueprint is an onboarding contract for devices that are not yet connected. It lets an operator define the initial management identity and the configuration components that should be associated with a model device or model HA cluster before the real appliance is discovered. FortiManager 8.0 extends this model so a certificate template can be selected in a blueprint, in addition to the existing provisioning, policy-package, fabric-authorization, pre-run CLI and HA settings.

Keep the objects distinct. A certificate template defines certificate-generation parameters. A Device Blueprint references that template and other reusable objects. A model device or model HA cluster is instantiated from the blueprint. The resulting device is still an offline model until discovery and authorization establish the managed-device relationship. The blueprint is not itself the installed FortiGate configuration.

Build order and provisioning flow

  1. In Device Manager, enable Certificate under Provisioning Templates feature visibility.
  2. Create the certificate template under Device Manager > Provisioning Templates > Certificate.
  3. Create a Device Blueprint from the Add Device menu and enable Certificate Template, selecting the template created in the previous step.
  4. Optionally bind a Fabric Authorization Template, Pre-run CLI Template, policy package, provisioning templates, folder, and HA parameters such as monitored and heartbeat interfaces.
  5. Add a model device or import devices from CSV using the blueprint. For an HA model, define the cluster password and interface roles consistently with the intended topology.

After the model device or model HA cluster is added, FortiManager generates the corresponding certificates, which can be inspected on the system:certificates page. That is a useful lifecycle boundary: template selection is declarative intent; certificate presence is evidence that the model-device creation path processed the template.

Configuration and scope

The blueprint can include System, IPsec, SD-WAN, static-route, BGP, CLI and IPS provisioning templates, or a template group. It can also assign a policy package and a folder. This means a single blueprint can establish a consistent first configuration for a branch class, but it also creates a dependency graph: referenced templates must exist, be visible, and be compatible with the target platform/ADOM.

Fortinet documents an important scope rule: editing an existing blueprint affects only devices added after the edit. Existing model devices are not retroactively rewritten. Treat a blueprint revision as a versioned onboarding profile, and do not assume a change to a template reference will repair already-created models.

Verification and troubleshooting

  • Confirm Certificate feature visibility is enabled and the certificate template exists before creating the blueprint.
  • Open the blueprint and verify the certificate-template field and other selected objects.
  • After adding a model device, inspect system:certificates for the generated certificate; absence points to the blueprint/template path, not a live-device installation problem.
  • For HA models, verify monitored interfaces, heartbeat interfaces, priority and cluster password separately from certificate generation.
  • After the real device is discovered, inspect the managed device configuration and installation preview to prove that the certificate is actually deployed or referenced as intended.

Operational use

Use separate blueprints for materially different branch classes, certificate identity requirements, and HA topologies. Keep certificate templates and blueprints under change control, test the full model-to-discovery-to-install lifecycle in a lab, and clone rather than casually editing a widely used blueprint. If an existing model lacks a generated certificate, compare its creation timestamp with the blueprint revision; changing the blueprint today will not retroactively fix yesterday's model. This avoids a common onboarding trap where the template is correct but the model object was instantiated before the template was attached.

lessons.title: Residual SQL analytics records after device deletion and controlled cleanup
lessons.body_html:
Why device deletion is not a data purge

FortiAnalyzer maintains more than one representation of log history. Raw log files and archive packets are stored separately from records inserted into the SQL analytics database. The Administration Guide documents a counter-intuitive lifecycle: deleting a device removes its raw log files and archive packets and records the action in the local event log, but it does not immediately delete the SQL rows already inserted for that device.

Consequently, a device can disappear from Device Manager while its older records remain queryable in Log View and FortiView and continue to influence reports. This is not necessarily a ghost device or a failed delete operation. It is a boundary between the device inventory, raw/archive storage, and analytics index. An operator who treats “delete device” as “erase all evidence” can make incorrect retention and compliance assumptions.

Data path and cleanup choices

When a log arrives, FortiAnalyzer can retain the raw/archive representation and insert a normalized record into the analytics database. Device deletion removes the raw/archive material associated with the device, but the SQL analytics rows remain until a separate cleanup path acts on them. The documented options are:

  • Rebuild the SQL database for the ADOM that owned the deleted device, or rebuild the entire SQL database. Rebuild is a database operation, not a device-delete retry.
  • Use the ADOM log storage policy. When the deleted-device rows age beyond Keep Logs for Analytics, or the analytics disk quota is exceeded, old analytics tables can be trimmed.
  • Use global automatic file deletion settings under System Settings > Advanced > Device Log Settings. These global settings can override other log-storage settings and apply across ADOMs.

Storage information separates Analytics and Archive usage. The two quotas and retention periods are not interchangeable. A change to log storage policy can affect current data ranges: Analytics rows may be purged, Archive logs may be reinserted into the database, and archive files outside the configured range may be deleted.

Verification: prove each layer separately

  1. Confirm the device is absent from Device Manager and locate the local event-log record for the deletion.
  2. Query Log View for the former device identity and a known time range. If rows remain, that is consistent with the documented SQL retention behavior.
  3. Inspect the ADOM's View Storage Info to compare Analytics and Archive quotas and their retention windows.
  4. Before a rebuild, determine whether historical analytics must be preserved for investigation or reporting. Record the affected ADOM and take the appropriate backup/change-control steps.
  5. After cleanup, repeat the same query and report test. A successful rebuild or retention change should be verified by the absence of the expected residual rows, not merely by a completed task message.

Failure modes and operational guidance

Do not rebuild the entire SQL database simply because one device was deleted. Prefer the affected ADOM when the cleanup scope is known. Do not reduce Keep Logs for Analytics without checking the effect on every device in that ADOM. If a report still contains the old device after deletion, first determine whether it is reading retained analytics rows; do not assume new log ingestion is still occurring. Conversely, absence of raw archives does not prove that analytics evidence has been removed.

The practical rule is to treat device inventory deletion, raw/archive deletion, and analytics-row cleanup as three different state transitions. Build decommission procedures that explicitly specify which evidence must remain, which evidence must be purged, and which FortiAnalyzer operation proves each outcome.

lessons.title: Layer-3 DHCP relay transaction: GIADDR, multiple relay targets and Option 82
lessons.body_html:
Purpose and relay object

A FortiSwitch Layer-3 interface can relay DHCP broadcasts from a client subnet to an external DHCP server. This is different from running a DHCP server on the switch: the relay forwards the client transaction and uses the DHCP/BOOTP gateway IP address field (GIADDR) to tell the server which client subnet needs a lease. The server must have a route back to the relay address so that its offer reaches the relay.

FortiSwitchOS supports up to eight relay targets per interface. Each target receives a copy of the DHCP message. If multiple servers respond, the client ultimately selects an offer; the relay does not merge scopes or guarantee that the first configured server wins. Option 82 can also be inserted to provide circuit/remote identity for policy or address assignment on the DHCP server.

Packet transaction

  1. The client broadcasts DHCPDISCOVER on its local VLAN.
  2. The FortiSwitch L3 interface receives the broadcast. If GIADDR is zero, the relay fills it with the relay agent/router address.
  3. If configured, the relay inserts Option 82 information.
  4. The relay forwards a copy to each configured DHCP server target.
  5. The server uses GIADDR to choose the matching scope. Option 82 can provide additional circuit/remote identity.
  6. The server sends DHCPOFFER to the relay address identified by GIADDR; the relay forwards the offer to the original client subnet.

This makes the server-side return route just as important as the relay's outbound reachability. A packet capture that shows DISCOVER leaving the switch proves only the first half of the transaction.

Configuration pattern

config system interface
    edit "v15-p15"
        set ip 192.168.15.1 255.255.255.0
        set dhcp-relay-service enable
        set dhcp-relay-ip "192.168.23.2" "192.168.23.3"
        set dhcp-relay-option82 enable
    next
end

The documented CLI fields are dhcp-relay-service, dhcp-relay-ip and dhcp-relay-option82. The GUI path is System > Network > Interface > Physical, then enable DHCP Relay and enter server addresses. Option 82 is optional. The DHCP server and DHCP relay cannot be enabled simultaneously on the same interface; DHCP snooping can coexist with a DHCP server, but that is a separate feature.

Evidence and troubleshooting

  • On the switch, verify the relay is enabled on the correct L3 interface and that the configured target list contains reachable DHCP server addresses.
  • Capture the client DISCOVER and verify GIADDR is the relay interface address. A zero or wrong GIADDR commonly leads to the wrong scope or no scope.
  • Inspect Option 82 only if the server expects it. An unexpected circuit ID can cause server policy to reject or misclassify a request.
  • On the DHCP server, confirm the scope selected from GIADDR and the offer destination. Check the route back to the relay address.
  • When multiple targets are configured, check each server's response and the client-selected offer rather than assuming all servers share identical scope configuration.

Operational boundaries

Use relay on the routed interface that owns the client subnet. Do not confuse Option 82 insertion with DHCP snooping's trusted-server database or with FortiAP per-VAP Option 82 construction. Keep the server's scope, GIADDR, and Option 82 policy aligned. During a migration, change one relay target at a time and capture a complete DORA exchange. A relay configuration that looks correct in the GUI is not proof of a completed lease; the complete evidence chain is DISCOVER, server scope selection, OFFER return, REQUEST and ACK.

lessons.title: SSID multicast enhancement and IGMP snooping: multicast-to-unicast replication and AP pruning
lessons.body_html:
Two related controls, two different jobs

Wireless multicast can waste airtime when every AP or client receives a stream that nobody on that radio needs. FortiAP provides two related controls. IGMP snooping tracks which multicast groups have listeners so the controller can prune APs without a listener. Multicast enhancement converts multicast traffic into per-client unicast transmissions, which can improve delivery to wireless clients because each copy can use a client-specific transmission rate and acknowledgement behavior.

Do not treat the controls as synonyms. IGMP snooping is membership-aware distribution: it prevents unrelated clients and APs from receiving groups they have not joined. Multicast enhancement is a delivery transformation: the AP maintains its own multicast client state and sends the payload as unicast to interested wireless stations.

Mechanics and threshold

When a client joins a multicast group, its IGMP membership is observed by the AP. The AP joins the corresponding group, and the controller can send multicast packets only to CAPWAP multicast groups that contain a listener. This prunes managed APs that have no multicast listener. With multicast enhancement enabled, the AP converts the stream into unicast copies for its clients.

The transformation has a capacity boundary. me-disable-thresh defines the client-count threshold for the SSID. If the number of clients on the SSID exceeds that value, multicast enhancement is disabled. The threshold is therefore not a multicast-group count or a bandwidth ceiling; it is a client population gate that changes the forwarding method.

Configuration pattern

config wireless-controller vap
    edit "example_wlan"
        set multicast-enhance enable
        set me-disable-thresh 32
        set igmp-snooping enable
    next
end

Fortinet documents that Advanced Wireless Features visibility must be enabled before configuring IGMP snooping from the GUI. In the GUI, edit the SSID under WiFi & Switch Controller > SSIDs and configure the Advanced Settings. The exact threshold should be based on expected peak associated clients and multicast behavior, not copied blindly from a lab.

Verification and evidence

  • Inspect the VAP configuration to prove the two features are enabled and the threshold is set.
  • Run diagnose wireless-controller wlac -c vap-mcgrp to inspect multicast group membership.
  • Capture traffic on the wired side and wireless side. A wired multicast stream may appear as multiple unicast copies over the air when enhancement is active.
  • Test with clients joining and leaving the group. A listener on AP-A should not cause AP-B without listeners to receive the group stream.
  • Increase client count past the configured threshold in a controlled test and confirm the expected change in enhancement behavior.

Operational failure analysis

If a wireless application misses multicast, first verify that the upstream network is actually forwarding the group to the FortiGate/AP path. IGMP snooping cannot create an upstream stream that never arrives. Then verify the client membership table and CAPWAP group delivery. If delivery changes only at high client counts, inspect me-disable-thresh before diagnosing RF interference. If every AP receives the stream, compare membership state and snooping configuration. If the stream reaches the AP but clients do not receive it, compare multicast versus unicast behavior and client group membership.

Use multicast enhancement selectively for workloads where unicast replication is beneficial, and size the threshold with airtime and client density in mind. The goal is not to force every multicast packet into unicast; it is to make group membership and wireless delivery behavior predictable under the expected SSID population.

lessons.title: Database Archive/Purge lifecycle, scheduled age-based retention and remote-backup dependency
lessons.body_html:
Purpose and data lifecycle

FortiNAC's Database Archive function applies age-based retention to selected log files. Eligible records are archived and then purged from the live FortiNAC database after the configured age time elapses. This is a lifecycle operation, not simply a backup copy. It has three distinct states: live records, archived records, and records re-imported for investigation.

Importing archived data is additive. FortiNAC adds the archived records back into the database; it does not overwrite existing records. This matters during an investigation because a restore is not a rollback to a historical database image. It is a rehydration of archived records into the current database context.

Scheduling and backup relationship

System Management groups Database Archive with backup/restore, HA, licensing and time-zone settings. The Archive/Purge task is scheduled and can be run on demand. The age time and schedule must be considered together: if the task runs less frequently than the retention window, records remain live longer than expected. The related local-backup setting is separate: “Remove local backups older than” removes local backup files from the FortiNAC server before they are copied to a remote server; it does not remove backups already stored remotely.

This separation creates a common operational trap. A remote backup can remain intact while local pre-copy backups are removed, and Archive/Purge can fail independently of the database's retention age. A historical Community troubleshooting example identifies a changed SSH key on the remote backup server as a cause of the Database Archive/Purge Failure Alert.

Operational sequence

  1. Define which log classes are eligible for archive and the age threshold.
  2. Configure the archive/remote backup destination and verify SSH identity if the workflow uses remote transfer.
  3. Set the scheduled Archive/Purge time and cadence so that the job runs before local storage pressure becomes critical.
  4. Run a controlled task and confirm the success event and archive artifact before assuming the live database was purged.
  5. If historical data is required, use Import Archived Data and verify the expected records were added without replacing current records.

Evidence and troubleshooting

  • Review the scheduled task result and Events & Alarms for Archive/Purge success or failure.
  • Use the remote backup configuration test to verify the SSH connection and host-key identity; a changed remote key can block the archive transaction.
  • Compare archive file timestamps with the age threshold and job schedule.
  • Check live database record counts or the relevant log view before and after the job to prove that eligible records were purged.
  • Check local and remote backup directories separately; the local cleanup setting does not delete the remote copy.

Recovery and safety

If the Archive/Purge failure alarm appears, do not manually delete database rows or remove backup files to reduce disk use. Verify the remote SSH key, repair the destination trust relationship, test the connection, and rerun the scheduled task. Confirm a success event and archive output. Before changing age thresholds, calculate the overlap between the retention period and task cadence. A setting that removes local backups after five days is unsafe if the remote copy task runs every fifteen days, because local copies can be deleted before they are transferred.

Keep database archive, database backup, and remote backup retention as separate controls. Archive/Purge controls aged log records; backup/restore protects system state; local-backup cleanup controls temporary copies. The engineer should be able to prove each operation independently.

lessons.title: FortiNAC-F 7.6.5 Microsoft Entra ID remote group mapping into User/Host Profile policy matching
lessons.body_html:
What the 7.6.5 change adds

FortiNAC-F 7.6.5 adds remote group mapping for Microsoft Entra ID. Groups configured in Entra ID become available for policy matching and appear under Who/What > Groups when an administrator builds User/Host Profiles. This turns cloud directory membership into a selectable NAC policy input; it is not the same as importing endpoint ownership metadata from an MDM connector.

The important object chain is identity source, group object, User/Host Profile, ordered endpoint-compliance policy, and endpoint-compliance configuration. The remote group is not itself the enforcement action. It is a condition that can help a profile match. The matched policy then selects the compliance configuration that determines which scan and agent treatment is applied.

Policy evaluation mechanics

FortiNAC-F evaluates endpoint-compliance policies in order. It compares the user and host with the User/Host Profile associated with each policy. When a match is found, the policy is applied and evaluation stops; the endpoint-compliance configuration inside that policy determines the treatment. A profile that matches every user and host is effectively a catch-all and makes lower policies unreachable.

This means a correctly mapped Entra group can still appear ineffective if the profile is wrong or a higher policy captures the endpoint first. Conversely, a group appearing in the group list proves the identity integration exposed the group, but it does not prove that the target user is a member or that a policy selected it.

Configuration and validation pattern

  1. Configure the Entra ID integration using the FortiNAC-F authentication cookbook for the supported release.
  2. Verify that the expected Entra groups appear in Who/What > Groups.
  3. Create or edit a User/Host Profile and select the remote group as a matching condition.
  4. Attach the profile to the intended endpoint-compliance policy and confirm the policy's order relative to local and global policies.
  5. Test with a user whose Entra membership is known, then inspect the matched profile and resulting compliance configuration.

Evidence and failure isolation

  • Group visible in Who/What > Groups: proves group discovery/projection, not user membership.
  • Test identity resolves to the expected remote group: proves membership context, not policy selection.
  • Policy evaluation shows the intended User/Host Profile as the first match: proves the decision point.
  • The selected endpoint-compliance configuration and scan result prove the enforcement action that followed the match.

If the group is absent, investigate the Entra integration and group retrieval before changing policy order. If the group is present but the policy does not match, check the test user's membership, profile fields, and the order of policies. If the policy matches but the endpoint is treated incorrectly, inspect the selected compliance configuration rather than the directory connector.

Operational boundaries

Keep remote group mapping distinct from MDM ownership-to-Host-Role mapping. The former supplies a directory group for identity policy matching; the latter maps device-management metadata into endpoint role state. Avoid using broad “Any” profiles above more specific Entra group policies. During rollout, test one group, one user and one policy before adding nested or overlapping group conditions. The value of the feature is a cloud-managed identity signal in the NAC decision chain, but the final enforcement result remains dependent on FortiNAC's own profile and policy evaluation.

lessons.title: Load-balancing HA synchronization contract: primary-owned objects, replicated authentication data and non-replicated services
lessons.body_html:
Two HA modes, different consistency contracts

FortiAuthenticator supports an active-passive cluster and an active-active load-balancing design. In cluster mode, configuration is synchronized between cluster members for failover. In load-balancing mode, one appliance is the Standalone Primary and up to ten geographically separated appliances operate as Load Balancers. Authentication requests can be distributed using round-robin DNS, NAS/client distribution, or an external load balancer.

Do not assume that active-active load balancing means full configuration replication. Fortinet documents that only a subset of authentication-related features can synchronize. The Standalone Primary is where shared users, groups and tokens are configured. Load Balancers receive only the selected synchronization categories. This is an explicit consistency contract, not a transient failure to copy every object.

What synchronizes

The documented load-balancing synchronization set includes users, groups, FortiTokens, certificates, MAC devices, realms, remote authentication servers, trusted subnets, SAML IdP, RADIUS Service, OAuth Service, TACACS+ Service and selected replacement messages for SAML IdP/OAuth. The primary administrator selects synchronized settings on the primary. The current state is visible at Dashboard > HA Status.

FortiAuthenticator explicitly states that some features, including FSSO, cannot synchronize between devices in load-balancing mode. A Community technical tip also documents that the LDAP tree and related settings are not synchronized in a load-balancing setup even though user information can synchronize. Treat that as an expected boundary, not proof that the whole HA channel is broken.

Configuration and traffic flow

  1. Choose Standalone Primary on the authoritative node and Load Balancer on each additional node.
  2. On each load balancer, configure the primary management IP and the shared key used for the encrypted synchronization channel.
  3. On the primary, add the load-balancer IPs and select the setting groups to synchronize.
  4. Configure request distribution separately using DNS, NAS/client distribution, or an external load balancer.
  5. Verify synchronization status and test each authentication service through each load-balancer address.

Up to ten load-balancers can be added. This supports geographically distributed authentication, but it also increases the importance of a consistent service inventory and explicit object ownership.

Evidence and troubleshooting

  • Dashboard > HA Status proves the primary-to-load-balancer synchronization state, not that every feature is replicated.
  • Compare user/group/token objects on primary and LB nodes, then separately compare LDAP trees, FSSO and other non-synchronized settings.
  • Test RADIUS, OAuth, SAML IdP and TACACS+ through each LB, not just through the primary.
  • If user authentication works on an LB but an LDAP tree is missing, check the documented sync scope before recalculating HA checksums or rebuilding the pair.

Design decision

Use load-balancing mode when geographically distributed authentication capacity is required and the deployment can operate within the documented subset of synchronized settings. Use active-passive cluster mode when full configuration synchronization and failover semantics are required. Some deployments combine an active-passive pair as the Standalone Primary with geographically separated load-balancers. The key design question is not simply “active-active or active-passive”; it is which configuration objects must be authoritative, which must replicate, and which services must be configured independently at each location.

lessons.title: Wildcard remote-user matching under Concurrent Logon licensing and auto-provision precedence
lessons.body_html:
Purpose and licensing boundary

FortiPAM 1.9.0 adds wildcard remote-user support for the Concurrent Logon license model. Instead of creating a static FortiPAM user entry for every temporary or rotating remote identity, an administrator can create a Remote User entry with “Match all users in a remote server or group.” The wildcard entry permits any remote user who matches the selected remote server or remote group to obtain a FortiPAM session under the mapped access model.

This is not a general wildcard for all authentication sources. The feature is documented as functional only with Concurrent Logon licensing. The user wizard also treats a remote group and a remote server as mutually exclusive selections. Choose the intended identity boundary explicitly rather than selecting both and expecting an OR match.

Matching and provisioning precedence

FortiPAM user types include Local User, API User, JWT User and Remote User. The wildcard option is a property of the Remote User type. At login, the remote identity is authenticated through the selected remote server/group and the wildcard entry matches the remote user without a per-user static record. Auto-provision rules take high priority when wildcard matching is enabled. This precedence matters in environments where remote groups and auto-provision rules can both create or map a user.

Wildcard entries must not be assigned to features that generate notifications, such as approval roles. A wildcard identity represents many possible people; notification-dependent approval workflows need a concrete recipient/approver mapping. Do not use a wildcard entry as a shortcut for an approval-role population.

Configuration and validation

  1. Confirm that the FortiPAM instance uses the Concurrent Logon license model.
  2. Go to User Management > User List and create a Remote User.
  3. Select the remote group or remote server that defines the identity population.
  4. Enable “Match all users in a remote server or group” and assign only roles/features supported for wildcard entries.
  5. Review Auto Provision Rules because their matching takes precedence over the wildcard mapping.
  6. Test with a known remote identity and a second temporary identity from the same group to prove the wildcard rather than a static user record handled the login.

Evidence and failure isolation

  • The user record shows the wildcard match option and the chosen remote server/group.
  • The license page confirms Concurrent Logon; a different license model is a feature eligibility failure, not a directory password failure.
  • Authentication logs show the remote identity and group result; FortiPAM session details show the effective user and role.
  • If a user receives an unexpected role, inspect auto-provision rules before changing the wildcard entry.
  • If the user can authenticate remotely but cannot launch a secret, inspect the session role and secret policy separately from the wildcard match.

Operational caveats

Wildcard users are useful for contractors, rotating operators and large remote groups, but they broaden the population that can enter FortiPAM. Keep the selected remote group narrow, avoid notification-generating approval roles, and test auto-provision precedence. Use explicit local or remote-user entries for identities that require individual approvals or notifications. The feature reduces identity-object administration; it does not remove the need for least privilege, secret-level access controls, session recording and launch approvals where those controls are required.

lessons.title: System-owned event timestamps and incident attributes: phRecvTime parser immutability
lessons.body_html:
Why receive time is system-owned

FortiSIEM records when an event is first received by the platform in the special phRecvTime attribute. That timestamp supports platform functions such as ingestion timing and event processing. FortiSIEM 7.5.1 documentation explicitly states that custom parsers cannot set phRecvTime. A parser that tries to manufacture or overwrite this value is changing system-owned metadata, not merely extracting a vendor field.

Keep source event time and platform receive time conceptually separate. The source timestamp describes when the device says the event occurred. The receive timestamp describes when FortiSIEM first received it. Their difference can expose clock skew, buffering, transport delay or collector queueing. If a parser overwrites receive time with source time, the platform loses that diagnostic distinction.

Event and incident data model

The pipeline is: raw event arrives at a Collector, FortiSIEM stamps receive time, the parser extracts vendor fields and normalizes the event, and the event enters search/correlation. Incident rules then create or update incident objects. FortiSIEM also reserves many incident attributes from user assignment because the platform may set or overwrite them. The 7.5.x documentation lists system-managed fields such as Event Type, Event Severity, Event Receive Time, Reporting IP/Device, Event ID, Parse Status, Incident ID/Status, first/last occurrence, clearing metadata, ticket fields and parser name.

These restrictions protect internal lifecycle state. A rule should populate supported user-defined incident attributes, not attempt to own fields that the incident engine controls.

Parser and rule design

When building a custom parser, map the vendor's event timestamp to the appropriate supported event-time field and leave phRecvTime untouched. When building an incident rule, select user-defined fields for enrichment rather than reserved platform fields. Review existing rules before upgrading to 7.5.x because rules that assign reserved attributes may need to be rewritten.

Verification

  • Use parser test output to compare the raw event timestamp with the normalized source event time.
  • Confirm that phRecvTime is generated by FortiSIEM and not assigned in the custom parser.
  • Compare source event time with receive time to measure ingest delay; do not interpret the receive timestamp as the device's event clock.
  • Validate incident rule actions after removing reserved fields. A successful event parse does not prove the incident action is valid.
  • For 7.5.1 enhanced search, note the separate release caveat that Search and Filtering do not work together in Rules, Reports and CMDB Devices; a Search can ignore active filters.

Operational troubleshooting

If ingestion latency suddenly becomes zero or negative after a parser change, inspect timestamp mappings before changing Collector time or NTP. If a rule fails validation or incident fields appear overwritten, compare the action list with the reserved attribute list. Preserve raw logs for before/after testing. The safe design is to let FortiSIEM own receive and incident lifecycle fields, while the parser owns vendor-specific event content and the rule owns supported enrichment fields.

lessons.title: Unstable Secure Private Access connection automation: conjunctive SLA, route-change and BGP-neighbor triggers
lessons.body_html:
Purpose and trigger semantics

FortiSASE includes a predefined automation event handler for an unstable Secure Private Access connection. The important behavior is its conjunction: the alert email is triggered only when SLA failures, routing changes and BGP-neighbor status changes all occur. This is not a generic “IPsec tunnel down” alert and not an OR condition in which any one signal is sufficient.

The handler is designed to identify a more meaningful instability pattern in the SPA control and data plane. A tunnel can flap without all three conditions being present. A routing change can occur without an SLA failure. A BGP neighbor can change state for reasons that do not correspond to a persistent service-connection issue. The predefined trigger waits for the combined signal set before notifying administrators.

Dependencies and configuration

The documented example requires proper SPA licensing and an already configured FortiGate acting as an SPA hub. In FortiSASE, open Operations > Administration > Automation. The Stitches tab is displayed; under Analytics event handlers, select “Unstable connection alert for Secure Private Access” and edit the action/recipient settings.

The network design uses FortiGate hubs for SPA with BGP per overlay by default or BGP on loopback. The hub and FortiSASE service connection must already be established. Do not troubleshoot the email handler before confirming that the SPA service connection and BGP control plane exist.

Test and transaction flow

  1. On the FortiGate SPA hub, identify the WAN interface and its SPA IPsec tunnel interface.
  2. In a controlled test, disable the tunnel interface. FortiSASE should show the corresponding SPA service connection with a configuration state indicating that all service connections have issues.
  3. Keep the tunnel down for approximately two minutes as in the documented example, then re-enable it.
  4. Confirm that the service connection returns to Success.
  5. In Operations > Administration > Automation, inspect Trigger count (last 7 days) and Last triggered. Verify the configured email recipient received the notification.

The signal chain is hub tunnel state and SLA telemetry, route-change telemetry, BGP-neighbor state, analytics event handler evaluation, then email action. FortiSASE sends an email for each Security PoP configured for the instance.

Evidence and interpretation

  • SPA service connection state proves the service connection's current health view, not that the email action ran.
  • Trigger count and Last triggered prove the event handler fired; they do not prove every recipient received the message.
  • Email receipt proves delivery to that mailbox, not that every Security PoP generated a separate alert.
  • Hub interface and BGP logs help establish which of the three trigger conditions occurred.

Failure isolation

If the tunnel is down but no alert appears, do not immediately assume the handler is broken. Check whether SLA failure, route change and BGP-neighbor status change were all observed. If only one or two occurred, the documented conjunction has not been satisfied. If all signals exist but the trigger count remains zero, verify the predefined handler is enabled and SPA licensing/hub prerequisites are met. If the trigger count increments but no email arrives, investigate action configuration and recipient delivery separately.

Use this handler for compound instability notification, and use lower-level tunnel/SLA monitoring for immediate single-signal alarms. The design intentionally favors a correlated instability event over noisy notifications from an isolated state change.

lessons.title: Local-out service routing through SD-WAN: interface-select-method, source identity and rule matching
lessons.body_html:
Forwarded sessions and local-out traffic are different paths

Secure SD-WAN is often validated with user traffic that enters a LAN interface and is forwarded through a firewall policy. FortiGate also originates its own traffic: DNS, NTP, central management, FortiClient EMS, DHCP relay, SCEP renewal, SNMP traps, NetFlow/sFlow, pings and probes. This local-out traffic does not begin as a forwarded user session. Its egress selection is controlled by the local service's interface-selection setting and the routing/policy path that follows.

FortiOS documents three interface-selection modes: auto uses the routing table to choose an outgoing interface, sdwan uses SD-WAN or policy-routing rules, and specify binds the service to a named interface. If an operator expects FortiGate-originated control traffic to follow an SD-WAN rule but leaves the service in auto mode, the packet may use ordinary routing instead.

Service-specific controls

Local-out settings are not one global switch. FortiOS exposes them in the relevant service configuration. For example, central-management traffic uses config system central-management; NTP server entries use config system ntp; FortiClient EMS uses config endpoint-control fctems; DHCP relay has an interface-level relay-interface selection; SNMP user/community hosts, NetFlow/sFlow collectors and IPS TLS active probing have their own selectors.

config system central-management
    set interface-select-method sdwan
end

config system ntp
    config ntpserver
        edit 1
            set interface-select-method sdwan
        next
    end
end

config system sflow
    config collectors
        edit 1
            set interface-select-method sdwan
        next
    end
end

For services that support a source-IP field, the source identity must be compatible with the SD-WAN rule. A rule matching a source subnet cannot match a packet whose source has not yet been selected or differs from the configured source.

DNS example and diagnostic boundary

A historical Fortinet Community scenario documents locally generated DNS traffic failing to match a source-specific SD-WAN rule when source-ip was not set under config system dns. The packet's source was unresolved at the point of matching, so the rule's source condition did not match. The old workaround was to define a source IP or match on destination instead. Treat that as a diagnostic example rather than a universal FortiOS 8.0 command recipe; verify the current DNS local-out GUI/CLI fields and actual packet source on the target release.

Evidence and troubleshooting

  • Inspect the service-specific interface-select-method and source-IP configuration.
  • Use diagnose firewall proute list to inspect policy-route entries and hit counters where applicable.
  • Capture the packet on candidate WAN members and confirm source address, destination, and actual egress.
  • Compare a local-out probe with a forwarded test flow. A forwarded session using the expected member does not prove that DNS/NTP/SNMP from the FortiGate uses the same path.
  • Verify the VDOM context for services whose local-out selector requires a VDOM.

Operational design

Inventory the FortiGate-originated services that must use a specific ISP, SD-WAN zone or source address. Configure each service explicitly and test it independently. Avoid matching on a source address that the service does not actually use. If local-out traffic must always use one WAN, specify that interface; if it should participate in SD-WAN steering, set the service to SD-WAN and validate the rule match. The control-plane traffic path is part of the WAN design, not an incidental detail.
